g.text: Environment & Energy
Renewable Energy & Transition
Should the use of single-use plastics be banned worldwide?
I believe that the use of single-use plastics should be banned worldwide.
A global ban is urgently needed to halt environmental degradation,
protect marine ecosystems, and accelerate the transition toward
a sustainable circular economy.
In conclusion, a worldwide ban on single-use plastics is essential.
By protecting ecosystems, saving marine species, and driving sustainable innovation,
humanity can safeguard the planet for future generations.
First and foremost, single-use plastics cause catastrophic damage to the environment
due to their non-biodegradable nature. Every year, millions of tons of plastic waste
accumulate in landfills and natural habitats. Over centuries, these plastics break down
into microplastics, which contaminate soil and water systems, ultimately threatening
biodiversity and entering the human food chain.
Secondly, plastic pollution poses a grave threat to marine life and oceans.
Sea turtles, fish, and seabirds frequently ingest plastic debris or become entangled in it,
leading to severe injury or death. Because ocean currents carry plastic waste across
international boundaries, individual national policies are insufficient. Only a unified
global ban can effectively stem the flow of waste into marine ecosystems.
Finally, banning disposable plastics incentivizes green innovation and sustainable practices.
Enforcing a global ban forces corporations to invest in biodegradable alternatives,
such as paper, glass, and plant-based polymers. This shift encourages consumers
and industries to adopt reusable products, fostering a culture of conservation.
While plastic pollution is a critical issue, I believe that an outright
global ban on single-use plastics is impractical and counterproductive.
A blanket prohibition imposes economic hardships, overlooks essential medical uses,
and ignores more realistic waste management solutions.
In conclusion, a total ban on single-use plastics is unrealistic.
Policy makers should instead focus on enhancing recycling infrastructure
and supporting technological development to achieve sustainable waste management.
To begin with, single-use plastics play an indispensable role in healthcare
and food safety. In medical settings, sterile plastic items such as syringes,
gloves, and IV bags are vital for preventing cross-contamination and saving lives.
Similarly, plastic packaging extends food shelf life and prevents foodborne illnesses.
Banning these materials without affordable substitutes would compromise hygiene standards.
In addition, a sudden global ban would inflict severe economic disruption,
particularly on developing nations and small businesses. Manufacturing scalable
alternatives like eco-friendly packaging remains expensive. Forcing poor countries
to replace cheap plastics overnight would strain local economies and inflate
the prices of essential consumer goods.
Lastly, the fundamental problem lies not in the material itself, but in improper
waste management. Rather than enforcing a total ban, international efforts
should focus on upgrading recycling technology, improving waste collection infrastructure,
and promoting responsible disposal practices worldwide.

Economy & Labor
(経済・労働)
Employment & Workplace
(働き方・労働環境)
Should companies adopt a four-day workweek?
I believe that companies should adopt a four-day workweek.
Transitioning to a shorter workweek offers substantial benefits
by improving employee well-being, boosting workplace productivity,
and enhancing talent attraction and retention in a competitive market.
In conclusion, adopting a four-day workweek is a advantageous strategy.
By prioritizing mental health, streamlining operations, and attracting top talent,
businesses can achieve long-term growth while improving employee satisfaction.
First and foremost, a four-day workweek significantly enhances work-life balance
and mental health. Prolonged working hours often result in chronic stress,
burnout, and fatigue among employees. Granting an extra day off allows workers
adequate time to rest, care for family members, and engage in personal hobbies,
which reduces absenteeism and leads to a healthier, more motivated workforce.
Secondly, reducing working days encourages higher operational efficiency.
When time is limited, employees naturally streamline daily tasks by eliminating
unnecessary meetings and reducing workplace distractions. Numerous trials have
demonstrated that staff can maintain or even surpass previous output levels
by focusing intensely during their remaining working hours.
Finally, offering flexible and reduced work schedules gives businesses a major
advantage in recruitment. Modern workers increasingly prioritize flexible lifestyle
options over marginal salary increases. Companies that implement a four-day model
can attract top talent and maintain high employee retention rates.
While a four-day workweek sounds appealing, I believe that companies
should not universally adopt this practice. Implementing a shorter
workweek creates severe operational hurdles, increases daily workplace stress,
and is unsuitable for many key industries.
In conclusion, a mandatory four-day workweek is unrealistic for many businesses.
Rather than enforcing a rigid model, companies should offer flexible working hours
that accommodate both industry demands and employee needs.
To begin with, compressing workload into four days often intensifies stress
during active workdays. If employees are expected to complete five days' worth
of tasks in fewer hours, daily workloads become extremely demanding. Longer daily
shifts can lead to physical exhaustion and heightened anxiety, defeating the original
purpose of improving employee well-being.
In addition, a four-day workweek is impractical for service-oriented and
continuous-operation sectors. Healthcare, customer support, logistics, and
manufacturing require constant coverage. Forcing a reduced schedule on these
industries would require hiring extra personnel to cover empty shifts, creating
unsustainable labor costs that could bankrupt small businesses.
Lastly, reduced operating hours can harm customer service quality and business
responsiveness. Clients expecting prompt communication may experience delays,
leading to frustration and lost revenue. In an increasingly interconnected global
economy, reduced availability can jeopardize international client relationships.

International Issues & Organizations
(国際問題・国際機関)
Role of International Organizations
(国際機関の役割)
Is the United Nations still effective in resolving modern global conflicts?
I agree with the view that the United Nations is still effective in resolving modern global conflicts.
Although the organization faces criticism for its limitations, it plays an indispensable role in maintaining
international stability and preventing large-scale warfare.
In conclusion, despite its political constraints, the UN remains an essential mechanism for peaceful
conflict resolution and humanitarian protection worldwide.
First, the UN provides a crucial diplomatic platform for ongoing dialogue between opposing nations.
Even during severe diplomatic crises, the UN General Assembly and Security Council allow world leaders
to communicate and negotiate. This continuous open communication prevents misunderstandings and reduces
the likelihood of reckless military escalation.
Second, the UN Peacekeeping Forces and humanitarian agencies significantly mitigate the human cost of wars.
While peacekeeping operations may not immediately end every armed confrontation, they protect civilians,
enforce fragile ceasefires, and distribute essential supplies in disaster-stricken areas. Agencies such as
UNHCR deliver lifesaving assistance to millions of refugees displaced by violent conflicts.
Finally, the UN establishes and enforces international legal frameworks that deter illegal aggression.
Through treaties and international courts, it sets global norms for human rights and war conduct,
holding aggressive regimes accountable over time.
I disagree with the assertion that the United Nations is still effective in resolving modern global conflicts.
Structural flaws within the organization heavily impair its capacity to enforce peace and stop ongoing warfare.
In conclusion, due to structural paralysis, lack of enforcement authority, and outdated conflict models,
the UN is no longer capable of effectively resolving contemporary global conflicts.
First, the veto power held by the five permanent members of the Security Council creates political gridlock.
Because these nation-states prioritize their own geopolitical interests, any binding resolution regarding major
global crises is routinely blocked. Consequently, the UN often remains paralyzed while devastating conflicts escalate.
Second, the UN lacks a standing military force to enforce its resolutions effectively.
Peacekeeping missions rely entirely on voluntary troop contributions from member states, and their mandates
are frequently restricted by political compromises. As a result, peacekeeping operations are often unable
to intervene directly to prevent atrocities or restore order in high-intensity war zones.
Finally, the nature of warfare has shifted from traditional inter-state disputes to complex non-state conflicts.
Modern wars frequently involve terrorist networks, civil militias, and cyber warfare, which the UN's traditional
diplomatic tools and international legal frameworks were never designed to handle efficiently.
Politics, Diplomacy & Security
(政治・外交・安全保障)
Refugee Crisis
(難民問題)
Should developed nations take in more refugees?
I believe that developed nations have a moral and economic responsibility
to accept a larger number of refugees. Expanding refugee admission
is crucial for upholding human rights, fulfilling international obligations,
and addressing domestic demographic challenges in wealthy societies.
In conclusion, developed nations should take in more refugees.
By fulfilling human rights obligations, alleviating labor shortages,
and promoting global cooperation, wealthy societies can foster a more compassionate
and prosperous international order.
First and foremost, accepting refugees is a critical humanitarian duty.
Millions of individuals worldwide are forced to flee their homelands due to
war, political persecution, and severe climate disasters. Developed countries,
possessing robust infrastructure and vast financial resources, are best positioned
to offer safety and legal protection to those seeking asylum from life-threatening situations.
Secondly, admitting refugees can yield substantial economic benefits for host nations.
Many advanced economies currently suffer from severe labor shortages
caused by aging populations and declining birthrates. Refugees bring diverse skill sets,
strong work ethic, and entrepreneurial spirit, which can revitalize struggling industries,
expand the tax base, and boost national productivity over time.
Finally, welcoming refugees enhances global stability and international cooperation.
Developing nations currently bear a disproportionate burden of the global refugee crisis
due to geographical proximity. When wealthy countries share this responsibility,
it eases geopolitical strain, fosters international goodwill, and strengthens
diplomatic alliances committed to regional peace.
While assisting vulnerable populations is important, I believe
that developed nations should not be pressured to accept more refugees.
Unrestricted refugee integration poses severe challenges to social cohesion,
strains public resources, and may compromise national security.
In conclusion, developed nations should prioritize domestic stability and regional aid
over increasing refugee intake. Addressing root causes abroad while maintaining
social cohesion at home represents a far more sustainable long-term strategy.
To begin with, accepting large volumes of refugees places immense pressure
on public infrastructure and welfare systems. Host governments must allocate
substantial funds for housing, healthcare, language instruction, and social assistance.
This financial burden can divert resources away from native citizens,
potentially provoking public backlash and political instability.
In addition, rapid demographic influxes can hinder social integration and cultural cohesion.
Significant differences in language, values, and social norms often lead
to friction between refugee communities and local residents. Without proper time
and resources for gradual assimilation, social polarization and cultural segregation
are likely to increase within host societies.
Lastly, mass refugee admissions present complex security and logistical challenges.
In times of crisis, thorough background checks become extremely difficult to execute,
raising concerns about potential security threats or illicit trafficking networks.
Rather than resettlement, developed nations should focus funding on regional aid
to address the root causes of displacement directly in crisis zones.

Society, Education
(社会・教育)
Education System
(教育制度）)
Should higher education be made completely free for all students?
I believe that higher education should be made completely free
for all students. Providing tuition-free tertiary education is essential
for promoting social mobility, fostering economic growth, and reducing
the growing burden of student debt in modern society.
In conclusion, making higher education completely free is a crucial investment
in a nation's future. By promoting meritocracy, boosting economic strength,
and lifting the debt burden from young workers, society stands to gain
immense long-term benefits.
First and foremost, making higher education free ensures equal opportunity
for all individuals regardless of their socioeconomic background.
High tuition fees often prevent talented students from low-income families
from pursuing advanced degrees, which perpetuates social inequality.
By eliminating financial barriers, universities can become truly merit-based,
allowing every capable student to realize their full potential.
Secondly, investing in higher education yields significant long-term economic benefits
for society as a whole. A highly educated workforce drives technological innovation,
increases national productivity, and attracts foreign investment. Furthermore,
graduates with higher qualifications generally earn more and pay higher taxes,
which ultimately offsets the initial public expenditure required to fund
free tuition programs.
Finally, removing tuition costs alleviates the crushing burden of student loans
that many young adults face upon graduation. High levels of debt force
new graduates to delay major life milestones, such as purchasing a home
or starting a family, which negatively impacts consumer spending.
Relieving this financial pressure allows young professionals to contribute
more dynamically to the economy from the start of their careers.
While the concept of free higher education sounds ideal, I believe
that university tuition should not be made completely free for all students.
Universal free tuition places an unsustainable burden on public finances,
threatens the quality of education, and disproportionately benefits wealthier families.
In conclusion, making higher education completely free is financially unsustainable
and counterproductive. Rather than granting universal subsidies, policy makers
should focus on targeted financial support to preserve academic quality
and ensure fiscal responsibility.
To begin with, funding higher education for all students requires immense tax revenue.
Governments attempting to implement free tuition must either raise taxes substantially
or divert public funds away from crucial infrastructure and healthcare programs.
This financial burden is particularly difficult to justify when many university
graduates already enjoy higher lifetime earning potential than non-graduates.
In addition, eliminating tuition fees can negatively impact the overall quality
of academic institutions. Without tuition revenues, universities become
overly dependent on government subsidies, which may fluctuate based on
political priorities. This financial constraint can lead to overcrowded classrooms,
underpaid faculty, and inadequate facilities, ultimately lowering academic standards.
Lastly, universal free tuition is an inefficient way to achieve social equity.
Students from affluent backgrounds who can afford tuition would receive
unnecessary government subsidies. Instead of making college free for everyone,
governments should focus resources on targeted financial aid and need-based scholarships
to assist low-income students who truly require assistance.
